answer.rationale: Finance's 18% cut is the binding constraint this cycle. memory_c2 tells me the low-cost vendor has already been onboarded once, cut unit cost sharply, invoiced accurately, and integrated quickly — so switching primary supply to them is not a cold-start gamble. memory_c6 shows the incumbent can offer volume pricing via multi-year commitment, but that lever requires negotiation time and a renewal window we do not have (14 days, no auto-renew) and would not hit 18% without further benchmarking. The assembly line at 94% with no buffer is the risk I must manage: switching primary vendor normally raises delivery risk, but c2's record of quick onboarding and accurate invoicing from the very vendor being quoted is the strongest evidence I have that the transition can be clean. memory_c3's second-source play is the right hedge for constrained components but is a separate risk vector, not the cost lever finance is demanding now, and I only get one move. Renewing the incumbent (c1) buys stability but cannot meet the mandate alone. Deferring (c5) preserves optionality but leaves us on month-to-month with a hard expiry in 14 days and no contract in place — that is the highest-risk option of all. So: switch primary vendor to the low-cost supplier now, secure the 18%, and queue a second-source addition for the constrained component at next review to rebuild the buffer we are running without.
